Topic 1 · Corporate Finance and Financial Markets

Outline

  • What Finance is about
  • Debt and Equity

What Finance is about

  • Corporate Finance addresses three questions: What long-term investments should the firm engage in? (Project finance, M&A…) · How can the firm raise the money for the required investments? (Corporate banking, Equity and Debt capital market…) · How much short-term cash flow does a company need? (Cash management, working capital management…)
  • A firm should create more cash flow than it uses. To create value, the financial manager should try to make smart investment decisions and smart financing decisions (your note: “= raising more money than it costs”). The size, timing and risk of the cash flows should all be evaluated.

Banks

  • The most well-known type of financial institution. Main activity: collect short-term deposits and transform them into long-term loans to individuals and businesses.

Investors

  • Investors trade financial assets on the market. Two types: institutional investors - companies or organizations investing their clients' money on their behalf - and retail investors - individuals investing their own money.
  • Institutional investors make up most of financial trading volumes, BUT retail trading has been rising quickly post-Covid, worldwide.

Institutional investors

  • They make investments on behalf of others: insurance companies (collect premiums and invest to cover future claims or collect savings, e.g. life insurance prod.), pension funds (invest retirement savings to pay future pensions), sovereign wealth funds (invest a country's revenues), endowment and foundations (charities and universities).
  • Delegated asset management: very often, institutional investors don't manage the money themselves, they delegate this task. Global third-party assets under management rose from $60 trillion (2013) to $121 trillion (2023) (source: McKinsey 2024).
  • Asset Management firms (e.g. Blackrock, Amundi etc.) set up investment vehicles (ETFs, mutual funds…) to invest on markets. Hedge funds and Private Equity funds: “alternative” investments accessible to a handful of investors.

Debt and Equity

  • Issuing debt is borrowing from creditors: the issuer (borrower) has the contractual obligation to make periodic fixed or floating interest payments to the bond holder (lender/creditor) and to repay the principal (face value) at maturity date.
  • Issuing equity is selling ownership of the firm.

Bond issuance vs. bank financing

  • Two main sources of debt: bank loans and corporate bonds.
  • Bank loans imply a systematic monitoring of borrowers, and a limited number of homogeneous lenders (mostly banks): prevalent among small, non-listed (private) firms.
  • Corporate bond is often an “unmonitored” lending with a pool of dispersed investors: prevalent among listed (public) firms and large private firms.
  • There are significant cross-country variations in the choice of debt. Bonds are securities, i.e. tradable financial instruments, just like stocks.

Financial Markets

  • Financial markets are where securities are traded. 2024 global market size: bond market $145 trillion > equity market $127 trillion (source: SIFMA 2025 Capital Markets Fact Book).

Fixed Income Markets

  • Global fixed income outstanding: $145.1T in 2024, up from $93.4T in 2014. The US is the largest market; China's share grew strongly over the decade.
  • Bonds can be issued by governments ⇒ sovereign bonds, and by firms ⇒ corporate bonds. The market for sovereign bonds is nearly twice as big as the one for corporate bonds.

Government vs. Corporate Bonds

  • A domestic-currency bond issued by a government is often referred to as a risk-free bond, because the taxing power (raise taxes or print money) allows the issuer to meet its obligations.

  • Corporate bonds (short-term and long-term) are issued by a corporate entity. The yield on a debt security is based on the risk-free rate with adjustments to capture: credit (default) risk [DP], liquidity [L], tax status [TA], special provisions [SP] (e.g. callable bond or convertible bond).

Corporate bonds and ratings

  • The difference between the yield on a debt security and the risk-free rate of the same maturity is called risk premium.
  • The firm's creditworthiness is the most important determinant of the interest rate the company will pay. Rating agencies (e.g. Standard & Poor's, Moody's, Fitch) perform credit analysis to measure default risk of specific issues and/or issuers; the result is a rating grade. Rating grades run from investment grade down to high-yield “junk bonds”.
  • Two stylized facts: the credit risk premium is a negative function of rating (the worse the rating, the higher the premium), and the risk premium of different ratings evolves over time.

Equity market

  • Global equity market capitalization: $126.7T in 2024, up from $69.0T in 2014; the US market is by far the largest (source: SIFMA 2025).

Equity

  • A share of stock represents partial ownership in a corporation. Shareholders are residual owners: they have a residual claim on the firm's assets if the company fails or is dissolved, after all debt and tax liabilities are paid.
  • Corporate stock offers investors a two-part rate of return: capital gains and periodical dividend payments. Two types of stock: common stock & preferred stock.

Equity analysis

  • Equity analysis is the equivalent of credit rating agencies for the equity market: equity analysts rate company stocks. They often work for the sales & trading division of an investment bank, but there are some independent research firms.
  • They give investment recommendations from “Sell” to “Buy” (or a similar wording) in the form of an “Analyst Note”; they forecast earnings and attend major corporate events (earnings announcements, M&A meetings…).
  • If you need detailed information about a company and its stock price performance (e.g. for an interview), look at analyst notes. ESSEC is a subscriber to the largest database on analyst reports: LSEG, through the K-lab website.

Topic 2 · The Additivity of Value (time value of money)

Outline

  • Compounding and Discounting

Compounding and discounting

  • Modern financial markets are a technology allowing the exchange of cash-flow streams between now and the future. A financial contract is, in essence, an exchange of cash-flow streams between now and some point in the future; its simplest form is the IOU: P paid today against F received tomorrow.
  • The implicit difference between P, paid today, and F, received tomorrow, is the interest rate: F = P + Interest = P × (1 + r), with r ≥ 0, determined by the interaction of many agents in financial markets.
One period: FV = C0 × (1 + r) · PV = C1 / (1 + r) NPV = PV of future cash inflows − PV of costs
  • Present value analysis and future value analysis should and must always lead to the same decision. The size, risk and timing of cash flows are all important.
  • Multi-period: leaving the money in the capital market and lending it for another year is called compounding: each interest payment is reinvested. $100 at 10 % becomes $110 after 1 year, $121 after 2, and FVT = 100 × (1.1)T after T years. In (1 + r)2 = 1 + 2r + r2, the term 2r is the simple interest over the two years and r2 is the interest on interest. « Money makes money, and the money that money makes makes more money » (Benjamin Franklin).

$100 invested at 10 %: simple vs compound interest.

FV = C0 × (1 + r)T — (1 + r)T is the future value factor PV = CT / (1 + r)T — 1 / (1 + r)T is the present value factor (r: discount rate)

Discounting refers to the process of calculating the present value of an amount to be received in the future.

  • How much to set aside today to have $100 five years from now at 10 %? x = 100 / 1.15 ≈ $62.09.
  • $5,000 deposited at 10 % grows to $10,000 when 1.1n = 2, i.e. n = ln 2 / ln 1.1 ≈ 7.27 years.
  • To cover $50,000 of university costs in 12 years with $5,000 invested today: (1 + r)12 = 10, so r = 101/12 − 1 ≈ 21.15 % per year.

Value is additive

  • The most important property of discounting is that value is additive: the present value of a set of cash flows is simply the sum of the present values of the individual cash flows, and the future value at T is the sum of the future values of the individual cash flows.
PV = Σt=0..T Ct / (1 + r)t FVT = C0(1 + r)T + C1(1 + r)T−1 + C2(1 + r)T−2 + … + CT
  • Example at 10 %: wealth of 1.5 M$ at time 0, income of 0.55 M$ at time 1 and 0.45 M$ at time 2 → PV = 1.5 + 0.55/1.1 + 0.45/1.12 ≈ 2.37 M$ ; FV2 = 1.5 × 1.12 + 0.55 × 1.1 + 0.45 = 2.87 M$.

Cash-flow map and NPV

  • To calculate the value of a stream of cash flows, first construct a cash-flow map: upward arrows indicate inflows (cash received), downward arrows indicate outflows (cash paid). NPV = PV of cash inflows − PV of cash outflows.
  • Contract example at 10 %: the contract pays $50 in 3 years and $100 in 5 years, and you must pay a fee of $20 one year from now. NPV = 50/1.13 + 100/1.15 − 20/1.1 = 37.57 + 62.09 − 18.18 = 81.48 > 0 : accept the contract.
Two conventions to refer to time: cash flows occur on exact dates, or during an interval (period). Unless specifically stated, assume cash flows occur at the end of the period (year, month, week, day…): date 0 = now = end of period 0, date 1 = end of period 1, and so on.

Stated vs. effective rates

  • Financial institutions quote rates according to conventions that differ across markets and products: in many cases the rate quoted is not the effective rate the client will receive or pay.
Compounding an investment m times a year for T years: FV = C0 × (1 + r/m)m×T Effective Annual Rate: EAR = (1 + r/m)m − 1 (the rate as if compounded once per year)
  • The stated annual interest rate is the annual rate without consideration of the compounding (sometimes called Annual Percentage Rate).
  • $50 invested at 12 % compounded semi-annually grows to $53 after 6 months, $56.18 after 1 year, and 50 × (1.06)6 = $70.93 after 3 years. Compounded quarterly instead: 50 × (1.03)12 ≈ $71.29.
  • Typical values of m: 2 (semiannual payments), 4 (quarterly), 12 (monthly), 250 (daily, working days only), 365 (daily). The higher m, the more often compounding happens, and the bigger the difference between the stated and the effective rate. The annual effective rate is the one that truly matters.
  • Continuous compounding (m → ∞, compounding every infinitesimal instant): FV = C0 × erT, where e ≈ 2.718 — the ex key on your calculator.
Terminology traps. « A 4 % interest rate compounded quarterly »: 4 % is the stated rate, the corresponding quarterly rate is 4 %/4 = 1 %, and the EAR is 1.014 − 1 = 4.06 %. « A 4 % interest rate compounded yearly »: in that case 4 % is the EAR. In France, mortgage rates are effective annual rates by law (taux annuel effectif global).

Simplification of formulas

  • Four standard financial contracts: perpetuity (a constant stream of cash flows that lasts forever), growing perpetuity (grows at a constant rate forever), annuity (constant stream for a fixed number of periods) and growing annuity (grows at a constant rate for a fixed number of periods).
Geometric series: a + aq + aq2 + aq3 + … + aqn = a × (1 − qn+1) / (1 − q) When q < 1 and n → ∞: a + aq + aq2 + … = a / (1 − q)
Perpetuity (starts next period): PV = C / r Growing perpetuity (grows after the first date): PV = C / (r − g) Annuity: PV = C × [ 1/r − 1 / (r (1 + r)T) ] = C × a(T, r) — the annuity factor a(T, r)
  • An annuity is valued as the difference between two perpetuities: one perpetuity that starts at time 1, less a perpetuity that starts at time T + 1.
  • Cash flows at the beginning of the period (annuity due): PV0 = CF1 + CF1 × a(r, T−1).
  • Cash flows that start at some period in the future (deferred annuity): value the annuity one period before its first payment (e.g. PV2 = CF3 × a(r, 5)), then discount that value back to date 0: PV0 = PV2 / (1 + r)2.
  • Cash flows neither consecutive nor equal: split the stream into blocks of equal consecutive cash flows, value each block as an annuity, then discount each block's value to date 0 and add. Example (CF2 paid in years 2-5, CF7 in years 7-9): PV0 = CF2 × a(r, 4) / (1 + r) + CF7 × a(r, 3) / (1 + r)6.
  • Interest rate not constant across periods: value each block with the rate that applies to its own periods, then discount each block's value back through the rates of the preceding periods. Example (rate r1 for years 1-3, r2 from year 4 ; CF2 in years 2-3 and 4-5, CF7 in years 7-9): PV0 = CF2 × a(r1, 2) / (1 + r1) + CF2 × a(r2, 2) / (1 + r1)3 + CF7 × a(r2, 3) / [(1 + r1)3 × (1 + r2)3].

Classic traps

  • Comparing offers on stated rates: always convert to EAR = (1 + r/m)m − 1 first.
  • Monthly payments with an annual stated rate: use r/12 per month and count periods in months.
  • PV = C/r assumes the first payment arrives next period; if it is paid immediately, add C.
  • A deferred annuity is discounted twice: once with the annuity factor, once back to date 0.

1. The Balance Sheet

  • The balance sheet is an accountant's snapshot of the firm's accounting value on a particular date, as though the firm stood momentarily still.
  • Shareholder's Equity ≡ Assets − Liabilities ⇔ Assets ≡ Liabilities + Shareholder's Equity.
  • Assets are economic resources owned by the company. They are listed in order by liquidity (the ease and speed with which assets can be converted to cash). The more liquid a firm's assets, the less likely the firm is to experience problems meeting short-term obligations. Liquid assets frequently have lower rates of return than fixed assets.
  • The liabilities and shareholders' equity side reflects the types and proportions of financing. They are listed in the order in which they must be paid. Generally, when a firm borrows it gives the bondholders first claim on the firm's cash flow. Shareholder's equity is the residual difference between assets and liabilities.

Book value vs. market value

  • Under GAAP, the accounting value (also called book value or carrying value) of the assets is in most cases recorded at historical cost adjusted for depreciation. Market value is a completely different concept: the price at which willing buyers and sellers trade the assets.
  • Management's job is to create a value for the firm that is higher than its cost. Many of the true resources of the firm do not appear on the balance sheet: good management, proprietary assets, favorable economic conditions, etc.

Net Working Capital (NWC)

  • NWC = short-term assets − short-term liabilities. When NWC is positive, the cash that will be available over the next 12 months will be greater than the cash that must be paid out.
Since Assets ≡ Shareholder's Equity + Liabilities: NWC = Shareholder's Equity + Long-Term Debt − Fixed Assets

4. Operating Working Capital Management

  • Two elements of the policy a firm adopts for short-term finance: the size of the firm's investment in current assets, and alternative financing policies for current assets.
  • Keep in mind the distinction between operating items and non-operating items. Example: the cash account usually contains operating cash (necessary to make payments related to the business) as well as excess cash, a non-operating item. The non-operating cash reflects a financing decision (the CFO could use it to pay back debt or pay a dividend) or a strategic decision (like the need to make an acquisition soon).
  • It is therefore preferable to define Operating Working Capital (OWC) as the difference between short-term operating assets and short-term operating liabilities.

Operating cycle and cash cycle

  • The need for OWC decision making arises because the typical business is characterized by unsynchronized cash inflows and outflows: it pays money to suppliers before receiving money from customers.
  • The operating cycle runs from raw material purchase to cash received: inventory period (raw material purchased → finished goods sold) + accounts receivable period (sale → cash received). The firm pays for material after the accounts payable period.
  • In practice, the inventory period, the accounts receivable period and the accounts payable period are measured by days in inventory, days in receivables and days in payables.
Cash Cycle = Operating Cycle − Accounts Payable Period

Optimal level of current assets: carrying costs vs. shortage costs

  • "Flexible" policy ⇒ high current asset needs: i. extended trade credit; ii. keep high inventory; iii. keep large amounts of cash balances and investments in marketable securities.
  • "Restrictive" policy ⇒ low current asset needs: i. refuse credit to customers; ii. keep low inventory; iii. keep low cash balances (borrowing when necessary) and no investment in marketable securities.
  • "Flexibility" costs money (low rate of return on short-term assets + cost of financing inventory: these are called carrying costs) but generates high future cash flow.
  • "Restrictive" policies entail risk (default on payments and loss of suppliers, running out of inventory and loss of customers: these are called shortage costs).

Financing current assets

  • It is crucial to distinguish between permanent and temporary requirements for current assets (seasonality). Once the business decision concerning current assets is made, the CFO must choose between temporary resources (short-term debt) and permanent resources (long-term debt) to finance them. Logically, the choice should depend on the type of assets being financed.
  • Maturity matching approach: current asset needs are financed with temporary resources, and permanent current asset needs (plus fixed assets) with permanent resources.
  • Aggressive approach: the firm finances part of its permanent current assets with temporary resources. Usually considered less expensive, because the term structure of interest rates is usually upward sloping - but more risky: i. interest rate risk; ii. refinancing risk; iii. risk of loss of autonomy. Bargaining power with respect to creditors is very much decreased: the firm is a bad customer from the bank's perspective.
  • Conservative approach: part of the temporary current assets is financed with permanent resources. This eliminates most of the risks of the aggressive strategy. From a cost perspective, it can make sense if the term structure is downward sloping and the firm has access to good short-term investment vehicles. Most of the time this strategy is costly: the firm holds excess cash invested in marketable securities. Bankers find this firm an excellent customer.

Factors to consider

  • The choice of the optimal current asset level, and of how to finance it, depends on many factors: 1. predictability of revenues; 2. seasonality of revenues; 3. competitive considerations; 4. bargaining power with respect to banks; 5. current term structure of interest rates; 6. planned future expenditures.

Topic 2 · The Additivity of Value (time value of money)

Outline

  • Compounding and Discounting
  • Stated and Effective Rates of Interest
  • Simplification of Formulas

Compounding and discounting

  • Modern financial markets are a technology allowing the exchange of cash-flow streams between now and the future. A financial contract is, in essence, an exchange of cash-flow streams between now and some point in the future; its simplest form is the IOU: P paid today against F received tomorrow.
  • The implicit difference between P, paid today, and F, received tomorrow, is the interest rate: F = P + Interest = P × (1 + r), with r ≥ 0, determined by the interaction of many agents in financial markets.
One period: FV = C0 × (1 + r) · PV = C1 / (1 + r) NPV = PV of future cash inflows − PV of costs
  • Present value analysis and future value analysis should and must always lead to the same decision. The size, risk and timing of cash flows are all important.
  • Multi-period: leaving the money in the capital market and lending it for another year is called compounding: each interest payment is reinvested. $100 at 10 % becomes $110 after 1 year, $121 after 2, and FVT = 100 × (1.1)T after T years. In (1 + r)2 = 1 + 2r + r2, the term 2r is the simple interest over the two years and r2 is the interest on interest. « Money makes money, and the money that money makes makes more money » (Benjamin Franklin).

$100 invested at 10 %: simple vs compound interest.

FV = C0 × (1 + r)T — (1 + r)T is the future value factor PV = CT / (1 + r)T — 1 / (1 + r)T is the present value factor (r: discount rate)

Discounting refers to the process of calculating the present value of an amount to be received in the future.

  • How much to set aside today to have $100 five years from now at 10 %? x = 100 / 1.15 ≈ $62.09.
  • $5,000 deposited at 10 % grows to $10,000 when 1.1n = 2, i.e. n = ln 2 / ln 1.1 ≈ 7.27 years.
  • To cover $50,000 of university costs in 12 years with $5,000 invested today: (1 + r)12 = 10, so r = 101/12 − 1 ≈ 21.15 % per year.

Value is additive

  • The most important property of discounting is that value is additive: the present value of a set of cash flows is simply the sum of the present values of the individual cash flows, and the future value at T is the sum of the future values of the individual cash flows.
PV = Σt=0..T Ct / (1 + r)t FVT = C0(1 + r)T + C1(1 + r)T−1 + C2(1 + r)T−2 + … + CT
  • Example at 10 %: wealth of 1.5 M$ at time 0, income of 0.55 M$ at time 1 and 0.45 M$ at time 2 → PV = 1.5 + 0.55/1.1 + 0.45/1.12 ≈ 2.37 M$ ; FV2 = 1.5 × 1.12 + 0.55 × 1.1 + 0.45 = 2.87 M$.

Cash-flow map and NPV

  • To calculate the value of a stream of cash flows, first construct a cash-flow map: upward arrows indicate inflows (cash received), downward arrows indicate outflows (cash paid). NPV = PV of cash inflows − PV of cash outflows.
  • Contract example at 10 %: the contract pays $50 in 3 years and $100 in 5 years, and you must pay a fee of $20 one year from now. NPV = 50/1.13 + 100/1.15 − 20/1.1 = 37.57 + 62.09 − 18.18 = 81.48 > 0 : accept the contract.
Two conventions to refer to time: cash flows occur on exact dates, or during an interval (period). Unless specifically stated, assume cash flows occur at the end of the period (year, month, week, day…): date 0 = now = end of period 0, date 1 = end of period 1, and so on.

Stated vs. effective rates

  • Financial institutions quote rates according to conventions that differ across markets and products: in many cases the rate quoted is not the effective rate the client will receive or pay.
Compounding an investment m times a year for T years: FV = C0 × (1 + r/m)m×T Effective Annual Rate: EAR = (1 + r/m)m − 1 (the rate as if compounded once per year)
  • The stated annual interest rate is the annual rate without consideration of the compounding (sometimes called Annual Percentage Rate).
  • $50 invested at 12 % compounded semi-annually grows to $53 after 6 months, $56.18 after 1 year, and 50 × (1.06)6 = $70.93 after 3 years. Compounded quarterly instead: 50 × (1.03)12 ≈ $71.29.
  • Typical values of m: 2 (semiannual payments), 4 (quarterly), 12 (monthly), 250 (daily, working days only), 365 (daily). The higher m, the more often compounding happens, and the bigger the difference between the stated and the effective rate. The annual effective rate is the one that truly matters.
  • Continuous compounding (m → ∞, compounding every infinitesimal instant): FV = C0 × erT, where e ≈ 2.718 — the ex key on your calculator.
Terminology traps. « A 4 % interest rate compounded quarterly »: 4 % is the stated rate, the corresponding quarterly rate is 4 %/4 = 1 %, and the EAR is 1.014 − 1 = 4.06 %. « A 4 % interest rate compounded yearly »: in that case 4 % is the EAR. In France, mortgage rates are effective annual rates by law (taux annuel effectif global).

Simplification of formulas

  • Four standard financial contracts: perpetuity (a constant stream of cash flows that lasts forever), growing perpetuity (grows at a constant rate forever), annuity (constant stream for a fixed number of periods) and growing annuity (grows at a constant rate for a fixed number of periods).
Geometric series: a + aq + aq2 + aq3 + … + aqn = a × (1 − qn+1) / (1 − q) When q < 1 and n → ∞: a + aq + aq2 + … = a / (1 − q)
Perpetuity (starts next period): PV = C / r Growing perpetuity (grows after the first date): PV = C / (r − g) Annuity: PV = C × [ 1/r − 1 / (r (1 + r)T) ] = C × a(T, r) — the annuity factor a(T, r)
  • An annuity is valued as the difference between two perpetuities: one perpetuity that starts at time 1, less a perpetuity that starts at time T + 1.
  • Cash flows at the beginning of the period (annuity due): PV0 = CF1 + CF1 × a(r, T−1).
  • Cash flows that start at some period in the future (deferred annuity): value the annuity one period before its first payment (e.g. PV2 = CF3 × a(r, 5)), then discount that value back to date 0: PV0 = PV2 / (1 + r)2.
  • Cash flows neither consecutive nor equal: split the stream into blocks of equal consecutive cash flows, value each block as an annuity, then discount each block's value to date 0 and add. Example (CF2 paid in years 2-5, CF7 in years 7-9): PV0 = CF2 × a(r, 4) / (1 + r) + CF7 × a(r, 3) / (1 + r)6.
  • Interest rate not constant across periods: value each block with the rate that applies to its own periods, then discount each block's value back through the rates of the preceding periods. Example (rate r1 for years 1-3, r2 from year 4 ; CF2 in years 2-3 and 4-5, CF7 in years 7-9): PV0 = CF2 × a(r1, 2) / (1 + r1) + CF2 × a(r2, 2) / (1 + r1)3 + CF7 × a(r2, 3) / [(1 + r1)3 × (1 + r2)3].

Classic traps

  • Comparing offers on stated rates: always convert to EAR = (1 + r/m)m − 1 first.
  • Monthly payments with an annual stated rate: use r/12 per month and count periods in months.
  • PV = C/r assumes the first payment arrives next period; if it is paid immediately, add C.
  • A deferred annuity is discounted twice: once with the annuity factor, once back to date 0.

1. The Balance Sheet

  • The balance sheet is an accountant's snapshot of the firm's accounting value on a particular date, as though the firm stood momentarily still.
  • Shareholder's Equity ≡ Assets − Liabilities ⇔ Assets ≡ Liabilities + Shareholder's Equity.
  • Assets are economic resources owned by the company. They are listed in order by liquidity (the ease and speed with which assets can be converted to cash). The more liquid a firm's assets, the less likely the firm is to experience problems meeting short-term obligations. Liquid assets frequently have lower rates of return than fixed assets.
  • The liabilities and shareholders' equity side reflects the types and proportions of financing. They are listed in the order in which they must be paid. Generally, when a firm borrows it gives the bondholders first claim on the firm's cash flow. Shareholder's equity is the residual difference between assets and liabilities.

4. Operating Working Capital Management

  • Two elements of the policy a firm adopts for short-term finance: the size of the firm's investment in current assets, and alternative financing policies for current assets.
  • Keep in mind the distinction between operating items and non-operating items. Example: the cash account usually contains operating cash (necessary to make payments related to the business) as well as excess cash, a non-operating item. The non-operating cash reflects a financing decision (the CFO could use it to pay back debt or pay a dividend) or a strategic decision (like the need to make an acquisition soon).
  • It is therefore preferable to define Operating Working Capital (OWC) as the difference between short-term operating assets and short-term operating liabilities.

Operating cycle and cash cycle

  • The need for OWC decision making arises because the typical business is characterized by unsynchronized cash inflows and outflows: it pays money to suppliers before receiving money from customers.
  • The operating cycle runs from raw material purchase to cash received: inventory period (raw material purchased → finished goods sold) + accounts receivable period (sale → cash received). The firm pays for material after the accounts payable period.
  • In practice, the inventory period, the accounts receivable period and the accounts payable period are measured by days in inventory, days in receivables and days in payables.
Cash Cycle = Operating Cycle − Accounts Payable Period

Optimal level of current assets: carrying costs vs. shortage costs

  • "Flexible" policy ⇒ high current asset needs: i. extended trade credit; ii. keep high inventory; iii. keep large amounts of cash balances and investments in marketable securities.
  • "Restrictive" policy ⇒ low current asset needs: i. refuse credit to customers; ii. keep low inventory; iii. keep low cash balances (borrowing when necessary) and no investment in marketable securities.
  • "Flexibility" costs money (low rate of return on short-term assets + cost of financing inventory: these are called carrying costs) but generates high future cash flow.
  • "Restrictive" policies entail risk (default on payments and loss of suppliers, running out of inventory and loss of customers: these are called shortage costs).

Financing current assets

  • It is crucial to distinguish between permanent and temporary requirements for current assets (seasonality). Once the business decision concerning current assets is made, the CFO must choose between temporary resources (short-term debt) and permanent resources (long-term debt) to finance them. Logically, the choice should depend on the type of assets being financed.
  • Maturity matching approach: current asset needs are financed with temporary resources, and permanent current asset needs (plus fixed assets) with permanent resources.
  • Aggressive approach: the firm finances part of its permanent current assets with temporary resources. Usually considered less expensive, because the term structure of interest rates is usually upward sloping - but more risky: i. interest rate risk; ii. refinancing risk; iii. risk of loss of autonomy. Bargaining power with respect to creditors is very much decreased: the firm is a bad customer from the bank's perspective.
  • Conservative approach: part of the temporary current assets is financed with permanent resources. This eliminates most of the risks of the aggressive strategy. From a cost perspective, it can make sense if the term structure is downward sloping and the firm has access to good short-term investment vehicles. Most of the time this strategy is costly: the firm holds excess cash invested in marketable securities. Bankers find this firm an excellent customer.

Factors to consider

  • The choice of the optimal current asset level, and of how to finance it, depends on many factors: 1. predictability of revenues; 2. seasonality of revenues; 3. competitive considerations; 4. bargaining power with respect to banks; 5. current term structure of interest rates; 6. planned future expenditures.

'alternative' investments accessible to a handful of investors
government-guaranteed vehicles
short-term deposit products

a discretionary choice to pay interest when profits allow
a contractual obligation to make periodic interest payments and repay the principal at maturity
to give creditors a voting seat on the board
an obligation lasting the infinite life of the security

bank loans are unmonitored lending used by listed firms; bonds are monitored lending used by small private firms

both involve the same pool of homogeneous lenders
bonds are not tradable, unlike bank loans

equal at about $135 trillion each
$145 trillion for bonds, $127 trillion for equity
$93 trillion for bonds, $69 trillion for equity

twice as big as the market for corporate bonds
half the size of the corporate bond market
limited to U.S. Treasury Bills
smaller than the equity market of France only

less than 1 year
1 year up to 10 years
10 to 20 years
more than 20 years

inflation only

the risk premium
the credit rating
the face value

capital gains and periodical dividend payments
coupons and maturity value
voting rights and dividends

measure the default risk of bond issues
rate company stocks and issue recommendations from 'Sell' to 'Buy' in an Analyst Note

Exercises 1-9 · short problems

Exercise 1 (1 point) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

Theo wants to have $55,000 for a down payment on a house seven years from now. He can either deposit one lump sum today or he can wait one year and deposit a lump sum. Assume an annual interest rate of 5.5 percent. How much additional money must he deposit if he waits for one year rather than making the deposit today?

Show the solution

PV1 − PV0 = $55,000 / (1+5.5%)6 − $55,000 / (1+5.5%)7 = $2,079.50

Exercise 2 (1 point) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

Sam just opened a savings account paying 4.5 percent interest, compounded annually. After four years, the savings account will be worth $6,000. Assume there are no intermediate deposits or withdrawals. How much money did Sam initially deposit into his savings account?

Show the solution

PV0 = $6,000 / (1+4.5%)4 = $5,031.37

Exercise 3 (1 point) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

If you invest $2,500 today, an investment guarantees you will have $3,600 four years from today. What rate of interest will you earn?

Show the solution

r = ($3,600 / $2,500)1/4 − 1 = 9.54 %

Exercise 4 (1 point) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

What is the stated annual percentage rate on a loan that charges interest of 1.65 percent per quarter?

Show the solution

APR = 1.65 % x 4 = 6.60 %

Exercise 5 (2 points) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

Christina will receive annuity payments of $1,200 a year for five years, with the first payment occurring at Year 4. What is the value of this annuity to her today at a discount rate of 7.25 percent?

Show the solution

The present value at Year 3 of the annuity is PV3 = $1,200 [(1 − 1/1.07255)/0.0725] = $4,887.48. It follows that PV0 = $4,887.48 / 1.07253 = $3,961.80

Exercise 6 (2 points) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

The Smart Bank wants to be competitive based on quoted loan rates and thus must offer loans at an annual percentage rate of 7.9 percent. What is the maximum rate the bank can actually earn based on this quoted rate?

Show the solution

For a given APR, the Effective Annual Rate is maximized with continuous compounding of interests. (1 + EAR) = e0.079, so EAR = e0.079 − 1 = 8.22 %

Exercise 7 (1 point) Official Mock Midterm Exam (Moodle)Official solution

Assume a cash flow of $82,400 in the first year and $148,600 in the second year. Also assume a present value of $303,764.34 at a discount rate of 12.75 percent. What is the cash flow in the third year if that is the only other cash flow?

Show the solution

$303,764.34 = $82,400/1.1275 + $148,600/1.12752 + C3/1.12753. It follows that C3 = $163,100

Hunter's Hut is considering a project that will require additional inventory of $48,000 and will increase accounts payable by $22,000. Show the solution

Show the solution

No: accounting rules partially prevent the administrator of a firm from recognizing as assets many intangible resources the firm may have. In addition, most of the assets are found at the historical cost, which may be different from the market value.

fr: Mock midterm · Topics 1–3 (18 Nov.)

Scope. Midterm: Wednesday 18 November, 9:00 (1h15); it covers topics 1, 2 and 3 only. The focus below follows the information you relayed on 4 Nov., not an official announcement: no questions on the career part; some questions with definitions and concepts; short exercises on topics 2 and 3.

Source. Every question and solution in this mock is written by Instinct from the course materials (booklet and official Practice Questions): these are not official exam questions. The official exercises stay unchanged in the Exercices tab.

Part A · Definitions and concepts

A1 · Who are the main actors in finance? Your example · Topic 1 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

Definition question relayed by you on 4 Nov.; correction written by Instinct from the course framework (RWJJ ch. 1, 15, 16).

The main actors are: households, who save and supply funds; non-financial firms, who demand funds to finance their investments; financial intermediaries (banks, insurance companies, investment funds), who channel the funds between savers and firms; and the financial markets (money market, capital market), where securities are issued and traded. Public authorities and regulators supervise the system.

A2 · Who are the institutional investors? Cite 3 of the main institutional investors. Your example · Topic 1 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

Definition question relayed by you on 4 Nov. (your exact example); correction written by Instinct.

Institutional investors are professional organisations that collect and invest large pools of money on behalf of households and firms, as opposed to individual (retail) investors. Three of the main ones: pension funds, insurance companies and mutual funds (asset managers). Hedge funds and sovereign wealth funds are other examples.

A3 · What is a financial contract? Topic 1-2 · session 1 booklet · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

Definition taken from your session 1 chapter (The Additivity of Value).

A financial contract is, in essence, an exchange of cash-flow streams between now and some point in the future; its simplest form is the IOU: P paid today against F received tomorrow. The implicit difference between P and F is the interest rate: F = P × (1 + r).

A4 · What is the difference between simple interest and compound interest? Topic 2 · session 1 booklet · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

Definition taken from your session 1 chapter (The Additivity of Value).

With simple interest, each year’s interest is computed only on the initial capital. With compound interest, each interest payment is reinvested, so interest itself earns interest (“interest on interest”). Example from the course: $100 at 10 % gives $120 after 2 years with simple interest, but $121 with compounding.

Part B · Short exercises (topics 2 and 3)

B1 · Topic 2 · You invest €2,000 today at 6 % per year, compounded annually. What is the value of your investment after 3 years? Topic 2 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

FV = C0 × (1 + r)T = 2,000 × 1.063 = 2,000 × 1.191016 = €2,382.03.

B2 · Topic 2 · What is the present value of €500 received at the end of each year for 4 years, at 8 %? Topic 2 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

Annuity: PV = C × [1 − (1 + r)−T] / r = 500 × [1 − 1.08−4] / 0.08 = 500 × 3.3121 = €1,656.06.

B3 · Topic 3 · A firm reports: end of 2025 — inventory €120, trade receivables €80, cash €50, trade payables €90 ; end of 2026 — inventory €150, trade receivables €110, cash €40, trade payables €100. What is the change in net working capital? Topic 3 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

You gave the example wording “What is the change on capital?” (4 Nov.): the exact metric was not specified, so this mock asks for net working capital, the quantity named in topic 3 (sources and uses of funds, working capital management). The same difference method applies to any capital aggregate; for shareholders’ equity: ΔEquity = Net income − Dividends + New shares issued.

Net working capital NWC = current assets − current liabilities.

Balance-sheet definition, cash included: 2025: (120 + 80 + 50) − 90 = 160 · 2026: (150 + 110 + 40) − 100 = 200, so a +€40 change.

For the sources-and-uses analysis, cash itself is excluded, because it is the residual being explained: 2025: (120 + 80) − 90 = 110 · 2026: (150 + 110) − 100 = 160. Change in NWC excluding cash = 160 − 110 = +€50: working capital increased by €50, a use of funds (it absorbs €50 of cash over the year).

B4 · Topic 3 · State whether each action increases, decreases or leaves cash unchanged: a. A dividend is paid. b. Common stock is issued. c. Merchandise is sold on credit. Topic 3 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

a. Decreases cash. b. Increases cash. c. No change (a sale on credit creates a receivable, not a cash inflow).

Same style as the official Practice Questions · Topic #3 (sources and uses of funds).

Annuity: PV = C × [1 − (1 + r)−T] / r = 500 × [1 − 1.08−4] / 0.08 = 500 × 3.3121 = €1,656.06.

B3 · Topic 3 · A firm reports: end of 2025 — inventory €120, trade receivables €80, cash €50, trade payables €90 ; end of 2026 — inventory €150, trade receivables €110, cash €40, trade payables €100. What is the change in net working capital? Topic 3 · Mock · written by InstinctSuggested solution
Show the solution

You gave the example wording “What is the change on capital?” (4 Nov.): the exact metric was not specified, so this mock asks for net working capital, the quantity named in topic 3 (sources and uses of funds, working capital management). The same difference method applies to any capital aggregate; for shareholders’ equity: ΔEquity = Net income − Dividends + New shares issued.

Net working capital NWC = current assets − current liabilities.

Balance-sheet definition, cash included: 2025: (120 + 80 + 50) − 90 = 160 · 2026: (150 + 110 + 40) − 100 = 200, so a +€40 change.

For the sources-and-uses analysis, cash itself is excluded, because it is the residual being explained: 2025: (120 + 80) − 90 = 110 · 2026: (150 + 110) − 100 = 160. Change in NWC excluding cash = 160 − 110 = +€50: working capital increased by €50, a use of funds (it absorbs €50 of cash over the year).

Show the solution

a. Decreases cash. b. Increases cash. c. No change (a sale on credit creates a receivable, not a cash inflow).

Annuity: PV = C x [1 − (1+r)^−T] / r

Effective annual rate of a loan Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

Find the Effective Annual Rate of a loan with an annual percentage rate of 18 % compounded monthly.

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

Monthly rate = 18 % / 12 = 1.5 %. EAR = (1 + 0.015)12 − 1 ≈ 0.1956 = 19.56 %.

Continuous compounding Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

Suppose you are investing $1,000 at a continuously compounded rate of 5 % for 5 years. What is the value of your investment at the end of 5 years?

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

FV = 1000 × e0.05 × 5 = 1000 × e0.25 ≈ $1,284.03.

British consol (perpetuity) Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

What is the value of a British consol that promises to pay £15 each year forever? Assume the annually compounded interest rate is 10 %.

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

Perpetuity: PV = C / r = 15 / 0.10 = £150.

Dividend stream (growing perpetuity) Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

The expected dividend next year is $1.30 and dividends are expected to grow at 5 % forever. If the discount rate is 10 %, what is the value of this dividend stream? What if the dividend is paid immediately?

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

Growing perpetuity: PV = C / (r − g) = 1.30 / (0.10 − 0.05) = $26. If the first dividend is paid immediately: PV = 1.30 + 1.30 × 1.05 / 0.05 = 1.30 + 27.30 = $28.60.

Car loan (annuity) Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

If you can afford a $400 monthly car payment for 3 years, how much can you afford to borrow if interest rates are 7 %, monthly compounded, on 36-month loans?

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

Monthly rate = 0.07/12 ≈ 0.5833 %. Annuity factor a(36, 0.5833 %) = [1 − (1 + 0.07/12)−36] / (0.07/12) ≈ 32.39. PV ≈ 400 × 32.39 ≈ $12,955.

Deferred annuity Session 1 bookletSuggested solution

What is the present value of a four-year annuity of $100 per year that makes its first payment two years from today if the discount rate is 9 %?

Show the solution

No official solution published: this solution applies the course formulas step by step.

One period before the first payment: PV1 = 100 × a(4, 9 %) = 100 × [1/0.09 − 1/(0.09 × 1.094)] ≈ 100 × 3.2397 = $323.97. Discount back one year: PV0 = 323.97 / 1.09 ≈ $297.22. Your handwritten computation rounds the annuity factor to 3.24, giving 324 / 1.09 ≈ $297.25 : same result, rounding aside.

Official practice questions and solutions from Moodle: questions (PDF) · solutions (PDF). Exercises from RWJ, Ross, Westerfield & Jaffe, Corporate Finance.

Q1 · Compute the future value of $1,000 compounded annually for: … Official practice questions Official solution

1. (RWJ, exercise 4.1) Compute the future value of $1,000 compounded annually for:
a. 10 years at 5%.
b. 10 years at 7%.
c. 20 years at 5%.
d. Why is the interest earned in part c. not twice the interest earned in part a. ?

Show the solution
a.      $1,000 × 1.0510 = $1,628.89
b.      $1,000 × 1.0710 = $1,967.15
c.      $1,000 × 1.0520 = $2,653.30
d.      Interest  compounds  on  the  interest  already  earned.    Therefore,  the  interest
earned  in  part  c,  $1,653.30,  is  more  than  double  the  amount  earned  in  part  a,
$628.89.
Q2 · A firm has a pension liability that will require the payment … Official practice questions Official solution

2. (RWJ, exercise 4.5) A firm has a pension liability that will require the payment of $1.5
million 27 years from today. If the firm can invest in a risk-free security that has a stated
annual interest rate of 8 percent, how much must the firm invest to be able to make the $1.5
million payment?

Show the solution
We have to find x, the amount the firm invests today for 27 years at 8% p.a. so that the
future value of this investment is $1.5 million.
X * 1.0827 = 1,500,000 ⇔ X  = 1,500,000 / 1.0827 = 187,780.23.
Q3 · You have won the Florida state lottery. Lottery officials … Official practice questions Official solution

3. (RWJ, exercise 4.6) You have won the Florida state lottery. Lottery officials offer you the
choice of the following alternative payouts:
Alternative 1: $10,000 one year from now.
Alternative 2: $20,000 five years from now.
Which one should you choose if the discount rate is
a. 0%?
b. 10%?
c. 20%?
d. What rate makes the options equally attractive to you?

Show the solution
      a.       At  a  discount  rate  of  zero,  the  future  value  and  present  value  are  always  the
same.  Remember, FV = PV (1 + r)  t.  If r = 0, then the formula reduces to FV = PV.
Therefore, the values of the options are $10,000 and $20,000, respectively.  You should
choose the second option.
      b.       Option one:   $10,000 / 1.1 = $9,090.91
                Option two:  $20,000 / 1.15 = $12,418.43
                Choose the second option.
      c.       Option one:   $10,000 / 1.2 = $8,333.33
                Option two:  $20,000 / 1.25 = $8,037.55
                Choose the first option.
d.       You  are  indifferent  at  the  rate  that  equates  the  PVs  of  the  two  alternatives.
You  know  that  rate  must  fall  between  10%  and  20%  because  the  option  you
would choose differs at these rates.  Let r be the discount rate that makes you
indifferent between the options.
                $10,000 / (1 + r) = $20,000 / (1 + r)5  ⇔ (1 + r)4 = $20,000 / $10,000 = 2
                  ⇔ 1 + r = 1.18921  ⇔ r = 0.18921 = 18.921%
Q4 · You are selling your house. The Smiths have offered you … Official practice questions Official solution

4. (RWJ, exercise 4.7) You are selling your house. The Smiths have offered you $115,000.
They will pay you immediately. The Joneses have offered you $150,000, but they cannot pay
you until three years from today. The relevant interest rate is 10%. Which offer should you
accept?

Show the solution
PV of Joneses’ offer = $150,000 / (1.1)3 = $112,697.22; Since the PV of Joneses’ offer
is less than Smiths’ offer, $115,000, you should choose Smiths’ offer.
Q5 · Suppose you place $1000 in an account at the end of each of … Official practice questions Official solution

5. (RWJ, exercise 4.9) Suppose you place $1000 in an account at the end of each of the next
4 years. If the account earns 12%, how much will be in the account at the end of 7 years?

Show the solution
There are many ways of solving this problem. Probably the safest one is the following:
find the present value of the 4-year annuity today, and then the future value in 7 years.
PV (today) = a(4 years, 12%) * 1000 = 1000 * 3.0373 = $3,037.3
FV (7 years) = 3,037.3 * (1 + 0.12)7 = $6,715.47
Q6 · Société Générale offers an annual 4.1% interest rate … Official practice questions Official solution

6. (RWJ, exercise 4.18) Société Générale offers an annual 4.1% interest rate compounded
quarterly, while BNP Paribas offers a 4.05% interest rate, compounded monthly. In which
bank should you deposit your money?

Show the solution
At SG the effective annual rate is (1 + r/4)4 – 1 = (1 + 0.041/4)4 – 1 = 0.04163.
At BNP the effective annual rate is (1 + r/12)12 – 1 = (1 + 0.0405/12)12 – 1 = 0.04126.
Société Générale is better.
Q7 · Assuming an interest rate of 10%, calculate the present value … Official practice questions Official solution

7. (RWJ, exercise 4.22) Assuming an interest rate of 10%, calculate the present value of the
following streams of yearly payments:
a. $1000 per year forever, with the first payment one year from today.
b. $500 a year forever, with the first payment 2 years from today.
c. $2,420 a year forever with the first payment 3 years from today.

Show the solution
      a.       $1,000 / 0.1 = $10,000
b.       $500  /  0.1  =  $5,000  is  the  value  one  year  from  now  of  the  perpetual  stream.
Thus, the value of the perpetuity is $5,000 / 1.1 = $4,545.45.
      c.       $2,420 / 0.1 = $24,200 is the value two years from now of the perpetual stream.
                 Thus, the value of the perpetuity is $24,200 / 1.12 = $20,000.
Q8 · What is the present value of end-of-year cash flows of $2,000 … Official practice questions Official solution

8. (RWJ, exercise 4.29) What is the present value of end-of-year cash flows of $2,000 p.a.
with the first cash flow received 3 years from today and the last one 22 years from today? Use
a discount rate of 8%.

Show the solution
PV (today)      = 2,000 * a(20years, 8%) / (1.08)2
= 2000 * 9.8181 / (1.08)2 = $16,834.88
Q9 · If the interest rate is 8%, what is the value at t=7 of a … Official practice questions Official solution

9. If the interest rate is 8%, what is the value at t=7 of a series of annual perpetual payments
of 100€ that will start being paid at the end of year 12? What is its value today?

Show the solution
The payments  begin  at  t  = 12. Their value at  the end of year 11 is  PV11=100 /  0.08 =
1250. The value of the payments at t = 7 is PV7 = PV11 / (1+0.08)4 = 918.787. The value
today (t = 0) is PV0 = PV11 / (1+0.08)11 = 536.136.
Q10 · Assume that the cost of a college education will be $20,000 … Official practice questions Official solution

10. (RWJ, exercise 4.38) Assume that the cost of a college education will be $20,000 per
year when your child enters college 12 years from now. You presently have $10,000 to invest.
What rate of interest must your investment earn to pay the cost of a four-year college
education for your child? For simplicity, assume the entire cost of the college education must
be paid when your child starts college.

Show the solution
FV (college education cost ) = 4 * 20,000 = 80,000 ⇔ PV = 10,000 = 80,000 / (1 + r)12
⇔ (1 + r)12 = 80,000 / 10,000  ⇔ 1 + r = 8(1 / 12) = 1.1892 ⇔ r = 18.921%
Q11 · You are saving for your retirement. You have decided that one … Official practice questions Official solution

11. (RWJ, exercise 4.42) You are saving for your retirement. You have decided that one year
from today each year you will place 2% of your annual salary in an account which will earn
8% p.a. Your salary is 50,000 € today, but it will grow at 4% p.a. throughout your career.
How much money will you have for your retirement which will begin in 40 years?

Show the solution
The safest way is to first find the present value of your future stream of savings and then
the  future  value  in  40  years.  Your  first  saving  will  be  equal  to  2%  *  50,000  *  1.04  =
1,040 € and then will grow at 4%
PV (savings) = [1,040 / (0.08 – 0.04)] * [1 - (1.04 / 1.08) 40] = $20,254
FV (40 years, at 8%) = 20,254 * (1.08) 40 = $440,011.07
Q12 · Now that you are earning good money at your new job, you … Official practice questions Official solution

12. Now that you are earning good money at your new job, you decided it’s time to buy a
house. The house of your dreams costs 300,000 € and the bank is willing to make you a
loan with a 25-year maturity. The bank advertises an annual stated discount rate of 5%,
with monthly payments (ignore inflation). Assume the 5% is monthly compounded.
a. The bank officer explains that, in order to obtain the loan, your salary (per month) must
be at least twice (2×) the amount of the monthly payment. What is the minimum salary
you must earn in order to obtain the loan? (Assume you start making the payments at
the end of next month).
b. Your monthly salary at your new job is 2,000 €. You also receive a bonus, paid once a
year, which is expected to grow by 4% annually. Your colleagues have just received
their bonus from last year, that was 6,000 € on average. All income is subject to 25%
tax. If you expect to stay 6 years on this job, what is the value of your employment
contract?

Show the solution
a.  Loan Present Value = 300,000
Number of payments (months) = 25 · 12 = 300
Monthly discount rate = 0.05/12 = 0.0041666
300,000  = CF · a(0.0041666, 300) ⇔ CF = 1753.77

You need to have a minimum salary of 1753.77 · 2 = 3507.54

b.  Salary net of taxes = (1–0.25) · 2,000 = 1,500 (per month)
    Number of payments (months) = 6 · 12 = 72
    Monthly discount rate = 0.0041666
PV of salary = 1,500 · a(0.0041666, 72) = 93,139.16

Bonus net of taxes =  (1–0.25) · 6,000 = 4,500
Bonus net of taxes next year = 4,500 · (1.04) = 4,680
Number of payments (years) = 6
    Yearly discount rate (effective rate) = (1+0.0041666)12–1 = 0.0511619
PV of bonus = 4,680 × [ 1/(0.0511−0.04) − (1.04)6 / ((0.0511−0.04) × (1.0511)6) ] = 26,019.43

Total value of contract = 93,139.16 + 26,019.43 = 119,158.6

Appendix: Some Useful Formulas

Annuity factor:                          a(T, r) = 1/r − 1 / (r (1+r)T)
Present value of an annuity:             PV0 = CF1 × a(T, r) = CF1 × [ 1/r − 1 / (r (1+r)T) ]
Future value of an annuity:              FVT = CF1 × [ ((1+r)T − 1) / r ]
Present value of a growing annuity:      PV0 = CF1 × [ 1/(r−g) − (1+g)T / ((r−g) (1+r)T) ]
Present value of a perpetuity:           PV0 = CF1 / r
Present value of a growing perpetuity:   PV0 = CF1 / (r − g)
Effective annual interest rate:          ra = (1 + ia/m)m − 1,   where ia = stated annual rate, m = number of sub-periods in a year.

11. (RWJ, exercise 4.42) You are saving for your retirement. You have decided that one year
from today each year you will place 2% of your annual salary in an account which will earn
8% p.a. Your salary is 50,000 € today, but it will grow at 4% p.a. throughout your career.
How much money will you have for your retirement which will begin in 40 years?

Show the solution
The safest way is to first find the present value of your future stream of savings and then
the  future  value  in  40  years.  Your  first  saving  will  be  equal  to  2%  *  50,000  *  1.04  =
1,040 € and then will grow at 4%

12. Now that you are earning good money at your new job, you decided it’s time to buy a
house. The house of your dreams costs 300,000 € and the bank is willing to make you a
loan with a 25-year maturity. The bank advertises an annual stated discount rate of 5%,
with monthly payments (ignore inflation). Assume the 5% is monthly compounded.
a. The bank officer explains that, in order to obtain the loan, your salary (per month) must
be at least twice (2×) the amount of the monthly payment. What is the minimum salary
you must earn in order to obtain the loan? (Assume you start making the payments at
the end of next month).
b. Your monthly salary at your new job is 2,000 €. You also receive a bonus, paid once a
year, which is expected to grow by 4% annually. Your colleagues have just received
their bonus from last year, that was 6,000 € on average. All income is subject to 25%
tax. If you expect to stay 6 years on this job, what is the value of your employment
contract?

a.  Loan Present Value = 300,000
Number of payments (months) = 25 · 12 = 300
Monthly discount rate = 0.05/12 = 0.0041666
300,000  = CF · a(0.0041666, 300) ⇔ CF = 1753.77

You need to have a minimum salary of 1753.77 · 2 = 3507.54

b.  Salary net of taxes = (1–0.25) · 2,000 = 1,500 (per month)
    Number of payments (months) = 6 · 12 = 72
    Monthly discount rate = 0.0041666
PV of salary = 1,500 · a(0.0041666, 72) = 93,139.16

Bonus net of taxes =  (1–0.25) · 6,000 = 4,500
Bonus net of taxes next year = 4,500 · (1.04) = 4,680
Number of payments (years) = 6
    Yearly discount rate (effective rate) = (1+0.0041666)12–1 = 0.0511619
PV of bonus = 4,680 × [ 1/(0.0511−0.04) − (1.04)6 / ((0.0511−0.04) × (1.0511)6) ] = 26,019.43

Total value of contract = 93,139.16 + 26,019.43 = 119,158.6

Appendix: Some Useful Formulas

Annuity factor:                          a(T, r) = 1/r − 1 / (r (1+r)T)
Present value of an annuity:             PV0 = CF1 × a(T, r) = CF1 × [ 1/r − 1 / (r (1+r)T) ]
Future value of an annuity:              FVT = CF1 × [ ((1+r)T − 1) / r ]
Present value of a growing annuity:      PV0 = CF1 × [ 1/(r−g) − (1+g)T / ((r−g) (1+r)T) ]
Present value of a perpetuity:           PV0 = CF1 / r
Present value of a growing perpetuity:   PV0 = CF1 / (r − g)
Effective annual interest rate:          ra = (1 + ia/m)m − 1,   where ia = stated annual rate, m = number of sub-periods in a year.

4. Comment on the following statement:
“The hypermarket business, contrary to perceived wisdom, is not a retail business: it is a
financial business.”

negative: most of the customers pay cash or debit card while the suppliers are paid with
a  long  delay  (90  days  or  more;  the  hypermarket’s  volume  helps  negotiating  very
favorable  terms  with  suppliers).  That  means  that  the  working  capital  needs  related  to

profitably  in  short-term  securities.  The  hypermarket  therefore  earns  considerable
amounts of interest on these funds, which more than compensates for the low margins it
charges on its products.

1. (RWJ, exercise 4.51) Southern California publishing Co. is trying to decide whether or not
to revise its popular textbook, Financial Psychobabble Made Simple. They have estimated
that the revision will cost $40,000. Cash flows from increased sales will be $10,000 the first
year. These cash flows will increase by 7 percent per year. The book will go out of print five
years from now. Assume the initial cost is paid now and all revenues are received at the end
of each year. If the company requires a 10 percent return for such an investment, should it
undertake the revision?

Show the solution
Just use the annuity formula.
NPV = – 40,000 +  10,000 [1 / (0.10 - 0.07)] [1 - (1.07 / 1.10)5 ] = 3,041.91
Revise the textbook.

are contingent on the economy as follows:

d. Calculate the expected risk premium.
e. (extra) Calculate the standard deviation of the market return. Calculate the standard
deviation of the risk premium (the market return net of the return on treasury bills).
Which is greater? Why?

Show the solution
       a. Expected Return on the Market = 0.25(–8.2%)+0.5(12.3%)+0.25(25.8%) = 10.55%
           Expected Return on T-Bills: = 3.5%
       b. Expected Premium = 0.25(-8.2-3.5)+0.5(12.3-3.5)+0.25(25.8-3.5) = 7.05%
       c. Variance of the market =
              = 0.25(–8.2% – 10.55%)2+0.5(12.3% – 10.55%)2+0.25(25.8% – 10.55%)2
= 0.01475625
           Variance of the risk premium =
              = 0.25*( (–8.2%–3.5%) – 7.05%)2 + 0.5*( (12.3%–3.5%) – 7.05%)2  
    +0.25*( (25.8% –3.5%) – 7.05%)2
= 0.01475625
The two must be equal, because the only source of variance in the risk premium is
the variance of the market. The reason is that, for two random variables,
Cov(X –Y) = Var(X) + Var (Y) – 2*Corr(X,Y)*σX*σY
If Y is not random, Var(Y) = 0 and Corr(X,Y) = 0 by definition, hence
Cov(X –Y) = Var(X).

Under the proposed capital structure, the firm will raise new debt in
the amount of: D = 0.40($325,000)
D = $130,000
This means the number of shares repurchased will be:

Shares repurchased = $130,000 / $65 = 2,000

Under the new capital structure, the company will have to make an interest
payment on the new debt. The net income with the interest payment will be:

NI = $37,500 – .08($130,000) = $27,100

This means the EPS under the new capital structure will be:

whether or not to convert its all-equity capital structure to one that is 40 percent debt.

to remain at $37,500 per year forever. The interest rate on new debt is 8 percent, and there are
no taxes.
1. Ms. Brown, a shareholder of the firm, owns 100 shares of stock. What is her cash flow
under the current capital structure, assuming the firm has a dividend payout rate of 100
percent?
2. What will Ms. Brown’s cash flow be under the proposed capital structure of the firm?
Assume that she keeps all 100 of her shares.
3. Suppose Star does convert, but Ms. Brown prefers the current all-equity capital structure.
Show how she could unlever her shares of stock to recreate the original capital structure.
4. Using your answer to part (c), explain why Star’s choice of capital structure is irrelevant.

D = $130,000
This means the number of shares repurchased will be:

Under the new capital structure, the company will have to make an interest

Shareholder cash flow = $903.33

Dividends received = $9.03(60 shares) = $542.00
The total cash flow for the shareholder under these
assumptions will be: Total cash flow = $208 + 542 = $750

This is the same cash flow we calculated in part a.

d.    The capital structure is irrelevant because shareholders can create their own leverage or
unlever the stock to create the payoff they desire, regardless of the capital structure the
firm actually chooses.
